query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount (around 1–2 at%) of silver into the high-entropy alloy will induce the formation of nanoscale, silver‐rich precipitates that segregate to wear surfaces during operation, thereby establishing a continuous, low-shear lubricious film which simultaneously reduces the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: The base high-entropy alloy (HEA) without silver, which exhibits conventional friction and wear behavior under sliding conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1–2 at% silver during alloy synthesis to achieve a uniform distribution that will favor in situ nanoprecipitation and surface segregation of silver during mechanical stress.
generation.conditions: Sliding or reciprocating wear conditions tested in ambient (or controlled atmospheres) across a broad service-temperature range (from room temperature up to approximately 400°C).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale Ag-rich precipitates within the HEA matrix that migrate to the contact surfaces under load and temperature, creating a continuous lubricious layer.
generation.mechanism: Silver has a low shear strength and a propensity for surface segregation. Under mechanical sliding, these Ag-rich precipitates coalesce at the interface to form a self-replenishing lubricious film that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby lowering friction and wear. This film remains stable across a wide temperature range, maintaining its low-shear properties and protection against wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated HEA, the silver-doped alloy is predicted to show a reduction in the coefficient of friction by roughly 30% and a wear rate reduction on the order of one to two magnitudes, with these improvements persisting consistently from room temperature to about 400°C.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy without silver addition, which exhibits higher friction and wear rates under similar testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect relies on maintaining the optimal silver concentration and achieving stable nanoprecipitate formation. Extremely aggressive environments (e.g., highly oxidizing or reducing conditions) or temperatures significantly beyond the tested range may alter the silver segregation behavior and compromise the lubricious film’s stability.
generation.uncertainty: While existing studies show that controlled nanoprecipitation (as in SCCPs) and the formation of protective surface films can improve mechanical properties and wear resistance, the precise quantitative improvement and long-term stability of a silver-induced lubricious layer in HEAs need to be empirically determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set with 1–2 at% silver addition and a control without silver. Subject both sets to pin-on-disk or reciprocating sliding wear tests across a temperature range from room temperature to about 400°C. Perform surface characterization (using SEM and EDS) post-test to check for the formation and continuity of the Ag-rich lubricious film.
measurements: Surface morphology and elemental mapping (to detect Ag segregation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silver-doped samples do not consistently show at least a ~30% lower COF and an order-of-magnitude reduction in wear rate compared to the control across the selected temperature range, or if the expected Ag-rich lubricious film is not observed on the worn surfaces, this would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening.
